items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: Lauren Daigle Has Released Christmas Music, So the Holiday Season Is Officially Open
items.author: RELEVANT Staff
items.summary: Every November, somewhere in a secure facility, a team of professionals gently thaws Mariah Carey so she can sing “All I Want for Christmas Is You” for the entire planet. Christian music has its own version of this tradition, and her name is Lauren Daigle. While nobody has to thaw her—she’s be
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Every November, somewhere in a secure facility, a team of professionals gently thaws Mariah Carey so she can sing “All I Want for Christmas Is You” for the entire planet. Christian music has its own version of this tradition, and her name is Lauren Daigle.

While nobody has to thaw her—she’s been out here the whole time, warm and ready—this weekend she released two more holiday songs, this time with the Preservation Hall Jazz Band: “Sleigh Ride” and “Go Tell It on the Mountain.”

If you feel like it is too early for this, please know that the paperwork has been filed. Halloween is over, the candy has been marked down to 50 percent, and the Christmas music season has legally begun.

For anyone keeping score at home, this is not a new hobby for her. Daigle’s first Christmas album, Behold, came out in 2016 and climbed to No. 29 on the Billboard 200. It also started a tradition: the Behold Christmas Tour, which returns this December for its 10th annual run. That is the real Mariah comparison. A holiday arrives, and so does Lauren Daigle, with a setlist and a very good coat.

The new songs are a pair of old favorites with a New Orleans accent. “Sleigh Ride” is the one that has been running through department stores since before you were born, and “Go Tell It on the Mountain” is the spiritual that has been spreading the Good News even longer than that. Preservation Hall brings the brass, the swing, and the general feeling that a very good party has broken out in a church basement. They also joined her last December for a holiday medley at the CMA Country Christmas special, so the chemistry was already on the record.

There is also a business angle, if you like those. It is her first release on Capitol, Interscope and CCMG, which is a lot of letters to put on one sleigh. The songs will come out on a 7-inch vinyl on Nov. 27, the day after Thanksgiving, so you can be a person who owns a Christmas record while also being a person who is still full of pie.

And if recorded music is not enough, the 10th annual Behold Christmas Tour opens Dec. 2 at the Ryman in Nashville, with stops in New Orleans and Orlando to follow. It is a beautiful room that was built for exactly this kind of evening, and it will probably smell like cinnamon candles and good intentions.

The thaw has happened, the songs are out, and the season has officially been declared open. Please enjoy your holidays responsibly, which in this case means having “Sleigh Ride” on rotation.

items.title: The Glory of the Unfinished: Reading Tolkien’s “Leaf By Niggle” on All Souls Day
items.author: Lindsey Weishar
items.summary:
Lindsey Weishar

This All Souls Day, Tolkien's “Leaf by Niggle” can help us reflect on purgatory with hope. What seems unfinished to us in this life may be continued in the next in ways beyond our imagining.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Lindsey Weishar

The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God . . . For though in the sight of others they were punished, their hope is full of immortality.

—Wisdom 3:1, 4

The Commemoration of All Souls marks a day of hopefulness, of coming together as a whole Church to intentionally pray for our faithful departed.

Though little is known about the experience of souls in purgatory, it’s been illuminating to read a couple literary explorations of this state: Dante’s Purgatorio, which aims to bring us through the landscape of purgatory; and, more recently, Tolkien’s short story, “Leaf by Niggle,” which does something similar with a focus on the journey of one (seemingly) ineffectual artist, Niggle, from life into the spaces beyond life.

What did Tolkien himself have to say about this story? In a letter to his publisher Stanley Unwin in early 1945, Tolkien writes the following: 

Since you have seen ‘Leaf by Niggle’—I was going to advert to it myself, as part apologia, part confession—I need say no more. Except that the story was the only thing I have ever done which cost me absolutely no pains at all. Usually I compose only with great difficulty and endless rewriting. I woke up one morning (more than 2 years ago) with that odd thing virtually complete in my head. It took only a few hours to get down, and then copy out. I am not aware of ever ‘thinking’ of the story or composing it in the ordinary sense. (Letter 98)

A few things are striking here. Unlike his typical experience with writing, this piece came to Tolkien pretty much complete. As a writer, when I hear this, I pay attention. The inspiration that involves little toil is rare, and for me, this is a sign that the piece is all the more meant to be shared because, as Tolkien alludes, the story comes from beyond him: “I am not aware of ever ‘thinking’ of the story or composing it in the ordinary sense.”

Secondly, his wry comment that “Leaf” is “part apologia, part confession” makes sense in light of other letters to his publisher. Tolkien struggled to keep up with the multitude of tasks daily life required, like teaching and marking papers at Oxford, tending to his family, and making progress on his translation and writing projects. The result was often burnout, health setbacks, and missed deadlines. So many of his letters to his publisher and colleagues begin with apologies for the delay in his response or deliverables, which for most of us probably feels all too relatable! In a letter from 1962, Tolkien complains to Rayner Unwin (who took over the business after his father) about the Puffin edition of The Hobbit in which the word “dwarves” was edited to read “dwarfs” (a real bother to Tolkien as an expert in philology) and notes a few other misprints. At the end of the letter, he says, “I am sorry to inflict such nigglings on you (I am a natural niggler, alas!) which will not seem to anyone else as important as they do to me.”

Niggle, too, is also taken up by details and struggles to manage time. We learn within the first two paragraphs of the story that he has a journey to make that he doesn’t want to make and that he is a rather unsuccessful painter because “he had many other things to do.” He’s often interrupted by his ailing neighbor, and, Tolkien tells us, “he was kind-hearted, in a way. You know the sort of kind heart: it made him uncomfortable more often than it made him do anything.” 

Typically a painter of individual leaves, readers learn Niggle has been captured by a greater vision:

There was one picture in particular which bothered him. It had begun with a leaf caught in the wind, and it became a tree; and the tree grew, sending out innumerable branches, and thrusting out the most fantastic roots. Strange birds came and settled on the twigs and had to be attended to. Then all round the Tree, and behind it, through the gaps in the leaves and boughs, a country began to open out; and there were glimpses of a forest marching over the land, and of mountains tipped with snow.  

The time for his journey comes, of course, at an unexpected hour. And the double pain of this moment is that his masterpiece is used for the utilitarian purpose of patching his neighbor’s roof.

We then enter into the strange purgatorial space that comprises the first stage of Niggle’s journey. There aren’t a lot of visual details in this space. Niggle is often in the dark. He’s tasked with odd jobs. All sense of time and place is lost. But here Niggle learns discipline: “He was becoming master of his time; he began to know just what he could do with it. There was no sense of rush. He was quieter inside now, and at resting-time he could really rest.”

Having experienced a healing of his relationship with time and rest, Niggle passes through this space into a vibrant and increasingly familiar place, which heals his relationships with others and his artistic vision. Niggle gets off a train and soon finds himself cycling through, wonder of wonders, the landscape of his own masterpiece! The great Tree he could not complete in life stands there complete. And what is more, he sees his leaves: “All the leaves he had ever labored at were there, as he had imagined them rather than as he had made them; and there were others that had only budded in his mind, and many that might have budded, if only he had had time.” 

Interestingly, this detail of the leaves leads him to think about his neighbor, Parish, not as an interrupter but as a collaborator. “Some of the most beautiful—and the most characteristic, the most perfect examples of the Niggle style—were seen to have been produced in collaboration with Mr. Parish: there was no other way of putting it.” Niggle realizes there are parts of this landscape that need “continuing,” and this work cannot be completed alone. “What I need is Parish,” Niggle says. “There are lots of things about earth, plants, and trees that he knows and I don’t. This place cannot be left just as my private park. I need help and advice: I ought to have got it sooner.” Parish appears and the two learn to work together as they were unable to when they were neighbors.

Order Your Set Today

What strikes me deeply about this story is the autobiographical detail that Tolkien shares in his letter to his aunt Jane Neave, to whom he sent a copy of “Leaf by Niggle” in 1962. After speaking about the ease of writing this piece and of a beloved poplar that inspired the great tree of Niggle’s world, he says: 

Also, of course, I was anxious about my own internal Tree, The Lord of the Rings. It was growing out of hand, and revealing endless new vistas—and I wanted to finish it, but the world was threatening. And I was dead stuck, somewhere about Ch. 10 (Voice of Saruman) in Book III . . . and I did not know how to go on. It was not until Christopher [his son] was carried off to S. Africa that I forced myself to write Book IV, which was sent out to him bit by bit. That was 1944. (I did not finish the first rough writing till 1949, when I remember blotting the pages . . . with tears as I wrote. I then myself typed the whole of that work all VI books out, and then once again in revision (in places many times), mostly on my bed in the attic of the tiny terrace-house to which war had exiled us from the house in which my family had grown up.) (241)

Taken alongside this detail, “Leaf by Niggle” almost reads prophetically. Tolkien, like Niggle, created a masterpiece, and like Niggle’s painting, it has become a place through which others have journeyed, healed, and dwelt for a time. At the end of “Leaf by Niggle,” Niggle’s life work, as experienced during his lifetime, is referred to as a “glimpse” of the real. It becomes a place for those making the journey to the Mountains (which though present within Niggle’s original picture also mark a place beyond it, a place that if not heaven, is closer to it). As one voice from the purgatorial realm says of Niggle’s picture-turned-place, “It is proving very useful indeed. . . . As a holiday, and a refreshment. It is splendid for convalescence; and not only that, for some it is the best introduction to the Mountains.”

It moves me greatly to ponder the role of the artistic life in Niggle’s purgatorial experience. That his art serves as a portal through which others pass on the road to salvation is incredible! Also incredibly encouraging is the possibility that what seems unfinished to us in this life may be continued in the next in ways beyond our imagining. Niggle is forgotten in the world, but his life as an artist is important in the next.    

In the 1962 letter to his aunt, Tolkien makes clear that “Leaf by Niggle” “is not really or properly an ‘allegory’ so much as ‘mythical.’ For Niggle is meant to be a real mixed-quality person and not an ‘allegory’ of any single vice or virtue.” And this person, in certain senses, bore resemblance to Tolkien. As his daughter, Priscilla Tolkien, explains it, 

[“Leaf by Niggle”] is autobiographical in that it concerns the life of an artist and how an artist is to respond both to the pressures of his absorption in his creative ideas and to the demands of living an ordinary life in the ordinary world; in other words how is he to enjoy living in the life of the imagination while at the same time remaining a moral being sensitive to the needs of other people. This was a situation my father faced throughout his adult life: he was the breadwinner in a family with four children, he earned his living by working extremely hard as an academic scholar and teacher, and for many years had to take on extra work in order to meet his financial commitments.

So, on this Commemoration of All Souls, “Leaf by Niggle” can help us reflect on purgatory with hope. While no work of fiction can encompass the reality of this state, its illustration via the imagination of the writer brings forth certain truths about the state itself. Jason M. Baxter’s comment on Dante’s imaginative rendering of purgatory in the introduction to his translation of Purgatorio could certainly be applied to “Leaf by Niggle”: “Purgatory is a place . . . where the green of the landscape is starting to get into the hearts of the penitent, in the form of hope.” 

What was given when Tolkien received this little story midway through his struggle with The Lord of the Rings was hope: hope that all his labors, and even his nigglings, would not be for nought, and hope that the Lord uses everything for our good.

Dr. Richard DeClue

The practice of praying for the dead, which we particularly emphasize during the month of November, has always been a part of the Church’s life.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Richard DeClue

Every November 2, the Church celebrates the Feast of All Souls (a.k.a., the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed). Typically, the entire month of November is a time when we collectively and consciously remember to pray for the dead even more intensively than we already do throughout the year.

In honor of this feast, I would like to highlight evidence in favor of praying for the dead in Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition. This ancient practice is, of course, connected to the Catholic doctrine of purgatory. After all, if there are souls in purgatory, then praying for them seems easily justifiable (at least to all but the most contrarian of interlocutors). Hence, I will count evidence for purgatory as evidence in favor of praying for the dead.

To start, I would like to consider the Jewish historical and religious context shortly before and during the time of Jesus. At that time, there were disagreements between different Jewish sects regarding the afterlife. As Carol Bakhos, professor of Jewish studies at UCLA, writes, “According to Josephus, Second Temple-period Jewish sects debated the reality of bodily resurrection. While the Sadducees and Essenes rejected the notion, the Pharisees adopted it. . . . In the Gospel of Mark, Jesus is said to have supported the Pharisaic view against that of the Sadducees.” In fact, as Bakhos reports in a separate article, “The Pharisees [and the Essenes] . . . believed in an afterlife in which reward and punishment would be meted out. The Sadducees, in contrast, rejected the notions of fate and of an afterlife.” In brief, the Sadducees did not believe in any afterlife (resurrected or otherwise); the Essenes believed in an afterlife but not in a bodily resurrection; the Pharisees believed in both. On this matter, Jesus affirms the position of the Pharisees. (Note: Some accounts say that the Essenes did believe in resurrection, but for our purposes, the dispute between the Sadducees and the Pharisees suffices.)

There is also evidence that some Jews during the Second Temple period believed in a kind of purgatory (intermediate state) as well as in intercession for the purification of souls therein. On this point, Kaufmann Kohler’s entry on “Purgatory” in the Jewish Encyclopedia cites a late first/early‑second century AD work called the Testament of Abraham: 

The idea of an intermediate state of the soul, release from which may be obtained by intercession of the saints, is clearly dwelt upon in the Testament of Abraham, Recension A, xiv., where the description is given of a soul which, because its good and its evil deeds are equal, has to undergo the process of purification while remaining in a middle state, and on whose behalf Abraham intercedes, the angels joining him in his prayer, whereupon the soul is admitted into paradise.

Kohler thinks such a belief is even more clear in teachings of the followers of the Pharisee named Shammai, who died around 30 AD. Kohler also cites a rabbinic source (Sifre Deuteronomy), which—although it dates to around the third or fourth centuries AD—purports to present earlier teachings: “The same view, that atonement should be made for the dead, is expressed in Sifre, Deut. 210.”

As Joe Heschmeyer remarks, “Jewish people before Jesus and the Jewish people today pray for the dead. . . . There’s differences in details, but the idea that those who die and are in an imperfect state of purification benefit from our prayers to make them right with God is very much a part of Jewish belief.”

A key piece of evidence for this is found in 2 Macc 12:38–45, which records events that took place around 163–161 BC during the Maccabean revolt. After a battle, Judas Maccabeus commands that the bodies of fallen soldiers be collected. It was then discovered that the deceased warriors had all been carrying “sacred tokens of the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids the Jews to wear.” In light of this tragic discovery, the survivors

turned to supplication, praying that the sin that had been committed might be wholly blotted out. The noble Judas . . . also took up a collection, man by man, to the amount of two thousand drachmas of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering. In doing this he acted very well and honorably, taking account of the resurrection. For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead. But if he was looking to the splendid reward that is laid up for those who fall asleep in godliness, it was a holy and pious thought. Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Macc 12:42–45).

In his book Truth is a Synthesis: Catholic Dogmatic Theology, Mauro Gagliardi argues, “The passage indirectly affirms that the dead may be found in the great beyond in a condition that is neither one of definitive salvation nor one of definitive condemnation. It is possible therefore to pray for them, so that they may be freed from the sin on the day of the resurrection. The Church always prays in the Liturgy for the living and also for the dead.”

Relatedly, an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia argues that practices attested to in the Memor-book of Nuremburg were “not borrowed from the Christian Church, but are a product of Jewish piety; for it has always been customary in Israel to remember the dead, to pray and to present offerings for them.” In fact, the authors of this entry claim that the Christian practice was rooted in early Jewish practice, noting that “many passages in the Church Fathers indicate that the prayers for the dead were Jewish in origin, and date from the time of the Apostles, who were Jews.”

There certainly is testimony in the Church Fathers affirming the practice of praying for the dead. Tertullian (d. 220 AD), commenting on Matt 5:25–26, interprets the passage as referencing what we would call purgatory. As Gagliardi reports, Tertullian 

had spoken of a place where the faults of sins are expiated prior to the corporeal resurrection at the end of times: “If we understand the ‘prison,’ of which the Gospel speaks, as the underworld, and ‘the last penny’ (Matt 5:26) as the smallest defect that has to be atoned for there before the resurrection, there will be no doubt that the soul suffers in the underworld some retributory penalty, without denying the complete resurrection, when the body also will pay or be paid in full [De anima 58]. (919). 

Elsewhere, Tertullian writes, “No one who ‘has journeyed away from the body,’ dwells immediately with the Lord, unless he is to turn aside thither from the privilege of martyrdom [De resurrectione carnis 43]” (Gagliardi, 919–920).

In Epistle 51.20, St. Cyprian of Carthage (d. 258 AD) compares and contrasts those who go immediately into heavenly glory with those who, though saved, must “by long suffering for sins . . . be cleansed and long purged.” Continuing, he says, “It is one thing, in fine, to be in suspense till the sentence of God at the day of judgment; another to be at once crowned by the Lord.”

Similarly, Pope St. Gregory the Great (d. 604 AD) teaches, “As for certain lesser faults, we must believe that, before the Final Judgment, there is a purifying fire. He who is truth says that whoever utters blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will be pardoned neither in this age nor in the age to come. From this sentence we understand that certain offenses can be forgiven us in this age, but certain others in the age to come” (referencing Matt 12:31; quoted in CCC 1031).

St. John Chrysostom lends an important Eastern Christian voice: “Let us help and commemorate them. If Job’s sons were purified by their father’s sacrifice, why would we doubt that our offerings for the dead bring them some consolation? Let us not hesitate to help those who have died and to offer our prayers for them” (Hom. in 1 Cor. 41:5; quoted in CCC 1032).

Mauro Gagliardi thinks that the early Christian liturgy is particularly important proof:

The ancient Christian custom (attested to from the very beginning) of praying for the deceased and celebrating the Holy Mass for them, as documented earlier, is even stronger evidence than these patristic attestations. How can one explain this custom if not for the conviction of faith, held without a doubt, that the dead can receive a benefit from such prayers? Faith in the existence of temporary penalties due to sins and not yet paid in life—penalties that must be satisfied after death and can also be satisfied through the prayers of the living—is thus implicitly expressed in this custom (920).
Magnificent Humanity
Get Pope Leo’s Encyclical

Jean-Hervé Nicolas concurs, “From the perspective of tradition, what is the most anciently attested . . . is prayer for the dead, especially the offering of the Eucharist for them. Here, the affirmation of purgatory is not found in a dogmatic formula but, instead, as a practice of prayer implying such an affirmation. Lex orandi, lex credendi” (Catholic Dogmatic Theology, book 2, 503).

Further evidence is found in the Christian catacombs dating as early as the first century up to the early fifth century. Some inscriptions are quite explicit about praying for the deceased, including prayers for “liberation from sin,” and, “sometimes the writers of the epitaphs request visitors to pray for the deceased,” according to the Catholic Encyclopedia. That entry rightly notes that “so overwhelming is the witness of the early Christian monuments in favour of prayer for the dead that no historian any longer denies that the practice and the belief which the practice implies were universal in the primitive Church.”

In brief, the practice of praying for the dead, which we particularly emphasize during the month of November, has always been a part of the Church’s life. We do well to add our prayers and sacrifices to those of the faithful throughout the centuries in supplication to God on behalf of all the souls that have departed before us. May they rest in the peace of Christ!

📖 Bible & Prophecy | The Land and the Book

Why memorize the Bible? After all, you can look anything up on your phone or tablet, right? That might be the prevailing thought of our times, but it CAN lead to a dangerous form of “Digital Amnesia.” We’re literally forgetting Scripture! It’s a problem we’ll address this week on The Land and the Book. Plus, we’ll have all the headlines from the Middle East—and some intriguing listener Bible questions.
